method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: The dollar sits near its highest since April 2025 because Federal Reserve officials keep backing more rate rises and markets see a December rise as close to certain. October retail sales released on Tuesday, November 17 showed US shoppers still spending, which keeps that bet in place ahead of the Fed's meeting minutes on Wednesday, November 18.

EUR.text: The euro slipped below $1.10 on Tuesday for the first time since April 2025, as expected US rate rises keep lifting the dollar. The European Central Bank is expected to raise rates once more in December and then stop, while the Fed looks set to keep going.

GBP.text: The pound sits near $1.32 after falling for most of the past week, as bets on more Federal Reserve rate rises lift the dollar. Tuesday's UK jobs report showed pay and job openings cooling but unemployment dipping, which leaves the Bank of England's expected December rate rise in place without giving the pound fresh support.

JPY.text: The dollar sits just under 160 yen because US rates are far above Japan's, and Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama has warned Tokyo will act against fast moves. On Tuesday a slide in stock markets sent some money into the yen as a safe place, pulling the dollar back toward 159, so the pressure on the yen has eased a little.

CHF.text: The Swiss franc sits near a one-month low against a dollar lifted by bets on more Federal Reserve rate rises. Monday's deeper slide in technology shares and continued Gulf tension add some demand for the franc as a safe place, which keeps the picture balanced.

CAD.text: Canadian inflation held at 3.1% in October, slightly below forecast, and the Bank of Canada's core measures sit near its 2% goal, so a December rate rise looks less likely. Oil, Canada's main export, keeps slipping toward $92 for Brent and the US dollar is strong, so the Canadian dollar has little to lean on.

AUD.text: The Australian dollar has been the weakest major currency this past month: the Reserve Bank of Australia's November rate rise was a 6-3 vote and big banks think rates have peaked, even though Governor Michele Bullock says inflation risks still lean higher. A deepening sell-off in technology shares adds to the pressure.

NZD.text: The New Zealand dollar sits near 55 US cents, held down by the strong US dollar and falling stock markets. The Reserve Bank says the country's banks can cope with rising global risks and a survey shows firms expect a rate rise soon, but neither has lifted the kiwi.

XAU.text: Gold is near $3,850 an ounce, around its lowest since October 2025, as markets bet on Federal Reserve rate rises and the dollar holds a 19-month high. Steady US consumer spending in October adds to that pressure, and war news from the Gulf has not drawn enough safe-haven buying to offset it.

OIL.text: Oil keeps drifting lower, with Brent near $92, because Middle East exports are recovering and the International Energy Agency expects more supply than demand this quarter. Attacks on Gulf shipping continue, including a tanker hit twice off Oman overnight, but move prices less each time; the OPEC+ meeting on November 29 on next year's output is the next big decision on supply.

items.headline: US dollar holds near 19-month high as retail sales support Fed rate hike expectations
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: US shoppers kept spending in October: retail sales rose 0.2% and the core measure rose a firmer 0.6%, which backs the case for a Federal Reserve rate rise in December.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve is raising rates to cool inflation, which sped up in October, and markets treat a quarter-point rise at the December 9 meeting as close to certain. Retail sales were the first big test of whether US consumers can handle higher borrowing costs.
beats.happened: Retail sales for October rose 0.2% from September, as expected, after a strong 0.8% gain the month before. The core measure, which leaves out cars, fuel, building materials and restaurants, rose 0.6%, more than forecast, and September's core figure was revised up to 0.5%. The dollar index held near its highest since April 2025.
beats.means: Spending is holding up despite higher rates, so nothing here argues for the Fed to stop. Markets now see almost no chance of a bigger half-point move, but a quarter-point rise stays the clear expectation.
beats.fx: The figures keep the support under the dollar in place rather than adding much to it. They also keep pressure on gold and on currencies like the euro whose central banks are closer to the end of their rate rises.

impact.why: Solid core spending backs a December Fed rate rise.
Firmer US rate expectations keep weighing on gold.
The gap between US and European rate paths stays wide.

items.watch: Minutes of the Fed's October meeting on Wednesday, November 18: signs of a split over more rate rises would test the dollar's climb.

items.headline: Risk-off trading boosts the yen; USD/JPY briefly falls to 158.90
items.story_title: The AI stock sell-off before Nvidia's results
items.summary: The yen gained in early London trading as falling Asian shares sent money toward safe currencies, pulling the dollar back from just under 160 yen.

beats.was: The dollar has climbed to near 160 yen because US interest rates are far above Japan's, and Japanese officials have warned they may step in near that level. A sell-off in technology shares hit Wall Street hard on Monday ahead of chipmaker Nvidia's results on Tuesday evening.
beats.happened: The dollar slipped from about 159.6 yen early in Tokyo to about 158.9 in early London as Asian shares and oil fell. The dollar index had touched a new high for the year in Asia before easing, and the euro bounced back above $1.10 after dipping below it.
beats.means: When shares fall sharply, investors tend to buy the yen as a safe place, and that is now pulling against the rate gap that has kept the dollar strong. The dollar's run paused before US retail sales and Nvidia's results.
beats.fx: A risk-off day helps the yen even without any Japanese action, and gives the dollar a brief breather after seven days up.

impact.why: Falling shares sent money into the yen, pulling the dollar off 160.
A pause in the dollar's seven-day climb ahead of US data and Nvidia results.

items.watch: Nvidia's results after the US close on Tuesday: another tech slide would likely add to yen demand.

items.headline: Dollar hits a fresh 19-month high in Asia; euro slips below $1.10
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: The dollar rose for a seventh day in Asian trading on Tuesday to its highest in 19 months, and the euro dipped below $1.10 for the first time since April 2025.

beats.was: US inflation sped up in October and several Federal Reserve officials have backed another rate rise at the December 9 meeting, which markets treat as close to certain. The dollar had already risen six days in a row.
beats.happened: The dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six major currencies, reached about 103.7. The euro touched about $1.0985, the pound sat near $1.318 and the dollar stayed just under 160 yen. Markets put the chance of a quarter-point Fed rise in December at about 90%, with a small chance of a half-point move.
beats.means: Nothing has yet challenged the bet on higher US rates, so the dollar keeps edging up. Tuesday's US retail sales figures are the first real test of whether American spending can carry more rate rises.
beats.fx: The euro losing $1.10 shows how wide the gap between US and European rate paths has become. The yen stays pinned near 160 mainly by the risk that Japan steps in to support it.

impact.why: A seventh straight gain on bets the Fed raises rates in December.
Below $1.10 for the first time since April 2025 as US rates are expected to rise faster than European ones.
The dollar sits just under 160 yen, held back only by the threat of Japanese action.

items.watch: US retail sales on Tuesday and the Fed's October meeting minutes on Wednesday: weak spending or a divided Fed would test the dollar's run.

items.headline: Banks call 4.85% rate peak despite Bullock's inflation warning
items.story_title: Has the Reserve Bank of Australia finished raising rates?
items.summary: Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Michele Bullock said the risks to inflation still lean upward and that the bank's rate rises were not only about oil. Major banks still think rates have peaked.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of Australia has raised its cash rate five times this year, to 4.85%, the highest in 18 years. Minutes out the same day showed the last rise was a 6-3 vote, and many in the market think the bank is done.
beats.happened: Speaking at a regulator's forum on Tuesday, Bullock said inflation risks remain tilted higher. She added that the bank began raising rates before the Middle East war pushed up oil prices, so the rises were about more than fuel costs. Big lenders including ANZ and Commonwealth Bank, along with Goldman Sachs, still expect 4.85% to be the top.
beats.means: Bullock is pushing back on the idea that the bank is finished, but she did not signal another rise. The next decision is on December 8, and the gap between her tone and the banks' forecasts leaves the outcome open.
beats.fx: A little support for the Australian dollar from a governor who sounds ready to act again, but it is outweighed by a split board and the strong US dollar.

impact.why: The governor's firm tone helps, but banks still see the peak and the board is divided.

items.watch: Australian wage figures on Tuesday evening US time and jobs figures on Thursday: strong numbers would back Bullock; weak ones would back the banks.

items.headline: New Zealand central bank warns global risks rising, says system can withstand them
items.story_title: Will the Reserve Bank of New Zealand raise rates on December 9?
items.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand said dangers to the world financial system keep growing, but New Zealand's banks are strong enough to cope. Strain on local households and firms has eased since last year.

beats.was: Twice a year the Reserve Bank of New Zealand reports on how safe the country's banks and borrowers are. Its policy rate is 2.75%, unemployment has risen to 5.7% and the bank decides on rates next on December 9.
beats.happened: In Tuesday's report the bank said global risks, including disruption to energy and trade from the Middle East conflict, are still building. It judged that New Zealand's financial system can absorb shocks, and said financial stress at home has come down from last year's peak, though unevenly across households and businesses.
beats.means: The report gives no reason to hold back on rates for financial-safety worries, so the December decision will turn on inflation and jobs. It adds little that is new for markets.
beats.fx: Close to neutral for the New Zealand dollar, which sat near 55 US cents and remains driven mostly by the strong US dollar.

impact.why: A sound banking system is reassuring, but warnings about rising global risk and a strong US dollar keep the kiwi low.

items.watch: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's rate decision on December 9.

items.headline: Dow sinks 739 points as Nvidia leadership crisis and Anthropic IPO jitters hit AI trade
items.story_title: The AI stock sell-off before Nvidia's results
items.summary: US stocks closed sharply lower on Monday: the Nasdaq fell 2.5% and the Dow lost 739 points as worries about chipmaker Nvidia and nerves over a planned record share listing by AI company Anthropic hit tech shares.

beats.was: Shares tied to artificial intelligence have led US stocks for about two years. Selling had been building for days before Nvidia, the biggest AI chipmaker, reports results after the US close on Tuesday.
beats.happened: By Monday's close the tech-heavy Nasdaq was down 2.5%, the S&P 500 1.0% and the Dow 739 points. The report links the drop to concerns about Nvidia's leadership and to unease about Anthropic's planned stock market listing, which would be the largest of its kind.
beats.means: The sell-off deepened through the day rather than fading, so investors are going into Nvidia's results already cautious. A further fall in stocks would usually pull money out of growth-linked currencies and toward safer ones.
beats.fx: Pressure on the Australian and New Zealand dollars, which tend to fall with stocks. The Swiss franc can gain from a move to safety; the yen less so, because Japanese rates are so low.

impact.why: A deeper stock sell-off weighs on a currency tied to global growth.
The same move away from risk hurts the New Zealand dollar.
Falling stocks add some demand for the franc as a safe place.
Safety buying could help the yen, but the wide gap with US rates still weighs on it.

items.watch: Nvidia's results after the US close on Tuesday: a strong report could steady stocks; a weak one could widen the sell-off.

items.headline: RBA board judges fifth rate hike needed to provide policy assurance
items.story_title: Has the Reserve Bank of Australia finished raising rates?
items.summary: Minutes of the Reserve Bank of Australia's early-November meeting show a 6-3 split: most members raised rates to be safe on inflation, while three feared a sharper slowdown. They gave no hint about December.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate on November 3 for the fifth time this year, to 4.85%, the highest in 18 years. Unemployment has climbed to a five-year high of 4.7% and house prices are falling.
beats.happened: The meeting record, out on Tuesday, shows six of nine members felt earlier rises might not be enough, because inflation has stayed above target for a long time and the economy still shows some strength. Three voted to hold, worried that rising joblessness and falling house prices could turn into a much sharper downturn.
beats.means: The board raised rates as insurance, not as the start of a new run, and a third of it already wants to stop. That fits market pricing that the peak has passed, with a small cut expected by the end of next year.
beats.fx: Little support for the Australian dollar: a split board and rate-cut pricing for 2027 leave it with less of a rate edge while US rates are expected to keep rising.

impact.why: A 6-3 split and no December hint back the view that Australian rates have peaked, while US rates are still climbing.

items.watch: Australian jobs figures and the fourth-quarter inflation reading: further rises in unemployment would strengthen the three members who wanted to stop.

items.headline: Oman discusses maritime security with Iran amid rising attacks in Strait of Hormuz
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: A tanker was hit twice off Oman overnight and its crew could not be accounted for, while Iran's foreign minister held talks in Oman on keeping sea routes safe.

beats.was: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran since late February, and the Strait of Hormuz, which carried about a fifth of the world's energy before the war, has seen repeated attacks on ships. Oil has still been falling because exports through the strait are recovering.
beats.happened: The UK navy's shipping-alert service said a tanker about 7 nautical miles off Khasab, Oman, was struck on Monday night, caught fire in its engine room, and was hit again later; the crew was reported unaccounted for. Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed two more ships hit naval mines in the strait, which has not been confirmed. In Muscat, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi discussed reopening dialogue and protecting shipping.
beats.means: Attacks on shipping keep coming, but traffic and oil prices have mostly shrugged them off. Oman's talks are a small sign that a diplomatic channel stays open.
beats.fx: Each new strike adds a little risk to oil supply, but with prices drifting lower on an expected glut, the push on oil and oil-linked currencies is small.

impact.why: Another tanker hit near Hormuz, though prices have shrugged off similar attacks.
Continued Gulf violence keeps some demand for safe currencies.

items.watch: Whether attacks spread to big crude carriers, and whether the Oman talks lead to any wider contact between Iran and the US.

items.headline: UK wage growth slows to 3.5% in three months to September
items.story_title: Bank of England: how far do rates rise?
items.summary: UK pay growth cooled a little more than expected and job openings fell to their lowest since 2021, but unemployment also dipped. The pound barely moved.

beats.was: The Bank of England raised rates in November for the first time in more than three years, because UK inflation is running well above its 2% goal. Markets expect another rise in December, and pay growth is one of the main things the Bank watches.
beats.happened: Regular pay, leaving out bonuses, grew 3.5% from a year earlier in July to September, down from 3.7% and just under forecasts. Unemployment slipped to 4.6% instead of rising, but the tax office's payroll count fell by about 34,000 in October and job openings dropped to 690,000, the fewest since early 2021.
beats.means: Slower pay and fewer openings point to a cooling job market, which takes a little heat out of inflation. It is not weak enough to change the Bank's December plans, so markets still see about a 90% chance of a rise.
beats.fx: A mixed report that leaves the December rate rise in place, so the pound keeps taking its lead from the strong dollar rather than from UK news.

impact.why: Pay and job openings cooled, but unemployment fell; December rise still about 90% expected.

items.watch: UK inflation for October, out Wednesday morning: a high reading would firm up the December rise.

items.headline: Oil slips on supply surplus outlook despite Gulf tensions
items.story_title: Oil supply: how much is lost to the war, and how fast it comes back
items.summary: Oil eased again early Tuesday, with Brent at $92, as traders focus on supply catching up with demand rather than on continued attacks on Gulf shipping.

beats.was: Oil prices jumped when the US-Iran war cut Gulf exports, but the International Energy Agency said on Friday the market returns to surplus this quarter as those exports recover faster than demand.
beats.happened: In early Asian trade Brent crude fell about 0.5% to $92.00 a barrel and US crude to about $85.30. Attacks on Gulf energy sites and ships, including in the Strait of Hormuz, continue. OPEC held an online meeting on Monday to review members' output capacity; the wider OPEC+ group meets on November 29 to set 2027 output. US emergency oil stocks have fallen to their lowest since 1982.
beats.means: The war premium in oil keeps shrinking because supply is coming back. The November 29 OPEC+ meeting matters more now: a decision to keep pumping would deepen the surplus.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil takes some support from the Canadian dollar and Norway's krone, and helps oil importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Recovering supply and a surplus outlook outweigh continued attacks on shipping.
Lower prices for Canada's main export trim the currency's support.

items.watch: The OPEC+ meeting on November 29 on 2027 output, and any confirmed damage to tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

items.headline: RBNZ Survey Shows Near-Term Inflation Fears Rising, but Long-Term Expectations Ease
items.story_title: Will the Reserve Bank of New Zealand raise rates on December 9?
items.summary: Business leaders and forecasters polled by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand now expect inflation of almost 3% over the next year, up from 2.6%. Their longer-run views eased, and they now expect the bank to raise its 2.75% rate soon.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand asks firms and economists every quarter where they see prices and rates heading. Its policy rate is 2.75%, inflation slowed to 3.7% in July to September, and unemployment has risen to 5.7%.
beats.happened: The November survey, out on Tuesday, showed expected inflation one year ahead rising to 2.92%. The two-year view, which the bank watches most, barely moved at 2.36%, and the five- and ten-year views fell. Respondents now see the policy rate at about 3.05% by the end of this year and 3.40% a year from now, and expect house prices to rise only 0.5%.
beats.means: Price worries are rising in the short run but the longer-run anchor is holding, which gives the bank room to move slowly. Respondents expect a rate rise at the December 9 meeting, but rising joblessness argues for caution.
beats.fx: A small lift for the New Zealand dollar from higher expected rates, but it was offset by the strong US dollar and the kiwi barely moved.

impact.why: Higher expected rates help, but steady long-run expectations and rising unemployment let the bank go slowly.

items.watch: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's decision on December 9: a rise would match what this survey expects; a hold would hurt the kiwi.

items.headline: Fed's Hammack reiterates case for slow, steady rate hikes -Bloomberg TV
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said on Monday inflation pressure is building, but she prefers raising rates in small steps. She added the Fed can move faster if it falls behind.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve's target range is 3.75%-4%, and markets expect a quarter-point rise at the December 8-9 meeting after a hot October inflation report.
beats.happened: In a Bloomberg TV interview, Hammack said she sees mounting inflation pressure but is not ready for a more aggressive path. She said she likes smaller moves, but the Fed could make larger ones if it gets behind on inflation.
beats.means: Another Fed official backs steady rises, which supports pricing for December and beyond. Her preference for small steps argues against the half-point move some traders have bet on.
beats.fx: Steady support for the US dollar from higher expected rates; it does not add to the case for a bigger December move.

impact.why: A Fed president backs more rate rises and keeps larger moves on the table.

items.watch: The Fed's October meeting minutes on Wednesday, for how many officials wanted to move faster.

items.headline: Canada's annual inflation rate holds at 3.1% in October
items.story_title: Will the Bank of Canada raise rates on December 9?
items.summary: Canadian inflation stayed at 3.1% in October, a touch below the 3.2% forecast. The Bank of Canada's preferred core measures sit close to its 2% goal, which weakens the case for a rate rise in December.

beats.was: Inflation in Canada was 3.1% in September, pushed up by fuel costs from the Middle East war. The Bank of Canada has said it is ready to raise rates if those energy costs spread into other prices, and it next decides on December 9.
beats.happened: Statistics Canada said prices rose 3.1% from a year earlier in October, against forecasts of 3.2%, and 0.2% from September. Without food and energy, inflation was 1.8%. The bank's own core measures came in at 2.0% for the median and 1.8% for the trimmed mean.
beats.means: Energy is lifting the headline number, but it is not spreading into everyday prices. That gives the Bank of Canada room to hold in December; bank ING sees January as the more likely time for any rise.
beats.fx: With fewer reasons for the Bank of Canada to act soon, the Canadian dollar has less support against a US dollar lifted by expected Fed rate rises. The US dollar was near 1.43 Canadian dollars, close to its October high.

impact.why: Slightly softer inflation and core near 2% make a December Bank of Canada rise less likely.
The gap between expected US and Canadian rate rises widens a little.

items.watch: Bank of Canada decision on December 9: a hold would confirm that energy costs are not yet a reason to raise rates.

items.headline: Gold falls to more than one-year low on resilient dollar as hawkish Fed bets build
items.story_title: Gold: rising US rates vs war risk
items.summary: Gold fell about 1% on Monday to near $3,840 an ounce, its lowest since October 2025, and silver dropped 3%. A strong dollar and expected Fed rate rises are outweighing demand linked to the Middle East war.

beats.was: Gold lost about 4.6% last week after US inflation figures for October came in hot and markets moved to price a December Federal Reserve rate rise as close to certain.
beats.happened: Spot gold slid to about $3,840 an ounce, briefly near $3,832, after an early bounce faded. Silver fell about 3% to $47.25, also a one-year low. The dollar index stood at its highest since April 2025, and Goldman Sachs cut its end-2027 gold forecast to $4,650.
beats.means: Higher US rates make gold, which pays no interest, less attractive to hold, and a dearer dollar makes it costlier for buyers abroad. Gulf attacks and tanker claims have not been enough to bring safe-haven buyers back.
beats.fx: Gold is moving with US rate expectations rather than with war news. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks on Monday, and minutes of the Fed's October meeting come on Wednesday.

impact.why: A fresh one-year low as bets on Fed rate rises firm and the dollar climbs.
The dollar index at its highest since April 2025 is the main weight on gold.

items.watch: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh on Monday: talk of further rate rises would keep pressure on gold.

items.headline: FOREX-Dollar hits highest since April 2025 as Fed rate bets lend support
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: The dollar rose for a sixth day in a row on Monday and closed New York trading at its highest since April 2025. The euro ended near $1.10, its weakest in 19 months.

beats.was: US inflation sped up in October and several Federal Reserve officials have said rates should rise again at the December 9 meeting. Markets treat that rise as close to certain.
beats.happened: The dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six major currencies, ended near 103.6. The euro finished around $1.100, the pound about $1.319 and the Australian dollar about 67.5 US cents. The dollar stayed just under 160 yen, a level where Japan has warned it may step in. Markets put the chance of a quarter-point Fed rise in December at about 93%.
beats.means: Nothing new happened on Monday to shake the bet on higher US rates, so money kept moving toward the dollar. The rise is steady rather than sharp, which shows a market leaning one way and waiting for a reason to change.
beats.fx: Broad support for the dollar; the euro, pound and Australian and New Zealand dollars all sit near multi-month lows against it. The yen is held near 160 mainly by the risk of Japanese action.

impact.why: A sixth straight daily gain on bets the Fed raises rates in December and again early next year.
The euro closed near $1.10, its lowest since April 2025, as the gap between US and European rate paths widens.
The dollar holds just under 160 yen; only the threat of Japanese intervention is keeping it there.

items.watch: US retail sales on Tuesday and the Fed's October meeting minutes on Wednesday: soft spending or a split Fed would test the dollar's run.

items.headline: Stock Market Midday, Nov. 16: Stocks Slide as Tech Selling Intensifies Across the Market
items.story_title: The AI stock sell-off before Nvidia's results
items.summary: US stocks fell on Monday as investors sold technology and chip shares ahead of Nvidia's results on Tuesday. Asian chip markets fell harder overnight, with Taiwan down about 6%.

beats.was: Technology shares tied to artificial intelligence have led stock markets for much of the past two years. Chipmaker Nvidia, the biggest of them, reports quarterly results after the US close on Tuesday, November 17.
beats.happened: By midday in New York the tech-heavy Nasdaq index was down 1.3%, the S&P 500 down 1.0% and the Dow 0.6%. Nvidia shares fell about 4% and memory-chip maker Micron about 6%. Overnight, Taiwan's main index dropped about 6% and South Korea's about 3.6%. US 10-year Treasury yields were near 5.1%.
beats.means: Investors are cutting risk before a big test of the AI story. When stocks fall broadly, money tends to leave currencies tied to global growth and drift toward safer ones; high US yields are adding to the strain on share prices.
beats.fx: Mild pressure on the Australian and New Zealand dollars, which tend to fall with stocks. The yen and Swiss franc can gain from a shift to safety, though the yen is held back by low Japanese rates.

impact.why: Falling stocks, especially the sharp drop in Asian chip markets, weigh on a currency tied to global growth.
The same move away from risk hurts the New Zealand dollar.
A broad stock sell-off adds some demand for the franc as a safe place.
Safety buying could help the yen, but the large gap between US and Japanese rates still weighs on it.

items.watch: Nvidia's results after the US close on Tuesday: a strong report could calm stocks, a weak one could deepen the sell-off.

items.headline: Warsh grapples with AI's potential economic impact, steers clear of its inflation risk
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh spoke about artificial intelligence on Monday and said nothing about inflation or the next rate move. That leaves markets leaning on other Fed officials, who have backed a December rise.

beats.was: US inflation sped up in October, and several Federal Reserve officials have said rates should rise again at the December 9 meeting. Markets had already priced that rise as close to certain.
beats.happened: Opening an AI and productivity conference at the San Francisco Fed, Warsh said AI could lift growth a lot, but warned it could also cost jobs or hit stocks if the payoff disappoints. He did not mention inflation and gave no view on where rates go next.
beats.means: Warsh chose not to push back on the December rise markets expect, so that pricing stands. His upbeat view of AI and growth hints he may be less eager than some colleagues to keep raising rates into next year, but he gave no signal either way.
beats.fx: No new push for the dollar, which stays near its highest since April 2025. The next Fed signal is the October meeting minutes on Wednesday.

impact.why: The Fed chair neither confirmed nor questioned a December rise, so dollar support from rate bets is unchanged.
No new rate signal from the Fed chair; gold stays near a one-year low on existing hike bets.

items.watch: Minutes of the Fed's October meeting on Wednesday: they show how many officials want more than one more rise.

items.headline: US November Empire manufacturing index 7.80 vs 18.00 expected
items.story_title: How strong is the US economy?
items.summary: A New York Fed survey of factories in New York State showed growth slowed sharply in November and new orders nearly stopped rising. Hiring, though, picked up to its fastest since mid-2022.

beats.was: The Empire State survey asks New York manufacturers whether business is getting better or worse; a reading above zero means more say better. In October it hit 25.5, a multi-year high.
beats.happened: The New York Federal Reserve said the main reading fell to 7.8 in November, well below forecasts. New orders dropped to 3.0 from 23.2. The hiring measure rose to 18.1, the highest since June 2022, and the measure of prices paid by factories eased to 45.9.
beats.means: Factory activity is still growing, but much more slowly, and the fall in new orders hints at softer months ahead. Strong hiring and still-high costs mean it does little to change the Fed's view that inflation needs more rate rises.
beats.fx: A small weight on the dollar on the day, but bets on a December Fed rise did not move. One regional survey rarely changes the picture on its own.

impact.why: Weaker factory orders point to slower growth, but strong hiring kept December Fed rate-rise bets intact.

items.watch: The Philadelphia Fed's factory survey on Thursday: a second weak reading would make the slowdown look broader.

items.headline: Eurozone industrial production rises less than expected in September
items.story_title: How weak is the eurozone economy?
items.summary: Factory output in the eurozone rose 0.2% in September, a little less than forecast, and was 1.5% lower than a year earlier. It was the first rise in four months but shows no real recovery.

beats.was: Eurozone industry has been shrinking for most of this year as high energy costs from the Middle East war and weak exports hold back factories, especially in Germany.
beats.happened: Eurostat, the EU's statistics office, said industrial production rose 0.2% in September from August, against forecasts of 0.3%, after a 0.5% fall the month before. From a year earlier, output was down 1.5%, a much bigger drop than the 0.2% expected. Dutch bank ING said it sees no sign of a real rebound.
beats.means: European industry is still weak, while inflation is running at about twice the European Central Bank's 2% target. That mix makes it harder for the ECB to keep raising rates after December, unlike the Fed.
beats.fx: Mild weight on the euro, which is already near its lowest since April 2025 against the dollar.

impact.why: Weak factory output supports the view that the ECB stops after one more rise, while the Fed keeps going.

items.watch: Eurozone business surveys (PMIs) later this month: another weak factory reading would add to the pressure on the euro.

items.headline: Pound extends slide as dollar firms on Fed rate-rise bets
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: The British pound fell for a sixth day in a row against the dollar, to about $1.32, as markets bet on more US rate rises. Analysts say US inflation, not anything in Britain, is driving the move.

beats.was: US core inflation for October came in above forecasts on November 10, and Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller then raised the idea of a larger half-point rate rise. The Bank of England raised its own rate earlier in November.
beats.happened: On Monday morning in London the pound slipped to about $1.319, heading for a sixth straight daily loss, and the euro hovered near $1.10. Two-year US interest-rate swaps have climbed about 0.35 percentage points since the inflation figures. Futures now lean toward quarter-point Fed rises in both December and January rather than one half-point move.
beats.means: Bank HSBC says the pound is being moved by US inflation rather than British news, so a firmer Bank of England has not been enough to hold it up. A bigger-than-expected euro-area trade deficit for September also gave the euro no help.
beats.fx: The dollar keeps gaining on both the pound and the euro, while the euro against the pound has barely moved this week. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks on Monday and minutes of the Fed's October meeting come on Wednesday.

impact.why: A sixth daily loss against the dollar as US rate expectations rise faster than Britain's.
Markets now price Fed rises in both December and January.
The euro sits near $1.10 and a wider trade deficit gave it no support.

items.watch: Fed minutes on Wednesday: a firm tone would back the January rise markets now expect and keep the pound under pressure.

items.headline: Oil falls as recovering Middle East exports bolster surplus outlook
items.story_title: Oil supply: how much is lost to the war, and how fast it comes back
items.summary: Oil slipped to about $95 for Brent on Monday as Middle East exports recover and Goldman Sachs forecast lower prices next year. Iran's claims of more tankers hitting mines near Hormuz gave only a brief lift.

beats.was: Oil fell sharply over the past two weeks after the International Energy Agency said the world will produce more oil than it uses this quarter, helped by a record release of emergency stocks.
beats.happened: By mid-morning in London, Brent crude was down 0.7% at about $95.15 a barrel and US crude near $88. Bank Goldman Sachs said on Sunday it expects Brent to average $88 next year and fall to $78 by the end of 2027. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two more tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz, which Reuters could not confirm. China's refineries processed 8% less crude in October than a year earlier.
beats.means: Markets are giving more weight to returning supply and weak Chinese demand than to unconfirmed attacks on shipping. Analysts at research firm BMI warn the recovery in Gulf exports is still fragile.
beats.fx: Lower oil takes some support from the Canadian dollar and Norway's krone, and eases inflation worries for big importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Recovering exports and a bank forecast of lower prices outweigh unconfirmed tanker attacks.
Softer oil trims support for Canada's main export.

items.watch: Whether the tanker-mine claims are confirmed by shipping firms or the US Navy; confirmed damage would bring the war risk back into prices.

items.headline: BOJ's Takata calls for swift hike in rates to 'good' position
items.story_title: Will the Bank of Japan raise rates in December?
items.summary: Hajime Takata, one of the Bank of Japan's nine rate-setters, said on Monday the bank should raise rates soon to a level that neither speeds up nor slows the economy. He lost a vote for a rise in October, so this is one member's view, not the board's.

beats.was: The Bank of Japan kept its rate at 1.25% in October, outvoting Takata, who wanted 1.5%. The yen is near its weakest in over a year at about 160 per dollar, and Japan's economy shrank slightly in July to September.
beats.happened: In a speech, Takata said the bank should move early and nimbly towards the neutral rate, which its staff put somewhere between 1.1% and 2.5%, aiming near the middle of that range. He warned that oil costs from the Middle East war could push inflation above 2% in the first months of 2027.
beats.means: At least one board member still wants rates well above today's 1.25%, so a December rise is not off the table despite the weak growth figures. Most of the board has so far preferred to wait.
beats.fx: A slight help for the yen, which edged up to about 159.4 per dollar on Monday, though the gap with much higher US rates still dominates.

impact.why: A Bank of Japan member pushing for early rate rises keeps a December rise possible, but he has lost this argument before.

items.watch: Whether Governor Kazuo Ueda or other board members echo Takata before the Bank of Japan's December meeting.

items.headline: China Industrial Output Slows to 4.8%, Retail Sales Growth Falls to 0.4%
items.story_title: The week's first numbers: Japan, China and Canada
items.summary: China's October figures for factory output, shop sales and investment all came in weaker than forecast, pointing to softer demand from the world's second-largest economy.

beats.was: China buys much of Australia's iron ore and much of New Zealand's farm exports, so its monthly spending and factory figures move both currencies. The economy grew 4.5% a year in July to September, better than expected.
beats.happened: Factory output grew 4.8% from a year earlier, down from 5.5% in September and below the 5.3% forecast. Retail sales rose just 0.4%, under the 0.8% expected, and investment in buildings and equipment fell 8.1% so far this year, a deeper drop than forecast, with property investment down more than a fifth. The statistics bureau said supply is still running well ahead of demand.
beats.means: Chinese households and businesses are holding back, and exports are doing most of the work. That raises the odds Beijing adds more support, but for now it means less demand for the raw materials Australia and New Zealand sell.
beats.fx: Negative for the Australian dollar, the currency most tied to Chinese demand, and mildly for the New Zealand dollar. A softer China also takes a little away from oil demand.

impact.why: All three main October measures missed, a clear sign of weaker demand from Australia's biggest customer.
Weak Chinese shop sales point to softer demand for New Zealand's food exports.
Slower factory and building activity in the biggest oil importer trims the demand outlook.

items.watch: Thursday's Trump–Xi–Putin meeting in Shenzhen; any sign of new Chinese spending support or trade relief would ease the hit to the Australian dollar.

items.headline: Oil prices fall on expectations of coming supply surplus
items.story_title: Oil supply: how much is lost to the war, and how fast it comes back
items.summary: Oil kept slipping early Monday in Asia as the market leaned on a forecast that supply will outrun demand this quarter, despite a new Iranian claim of a tanker hitting a mine.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since February and traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf's main oil route, is badly disrupted. Last week the International Energy Agency, which advises rich countries on energy, switched its view for October to December from a shortage to a surplus.
beats.happened: Brent, the world benchmark, fell about half a percent to near $95.40 a barrel and US crude eased to about $88.30. The agency expects supply to beat demand by 1.7 million barrels a day this quarter and says 71 million barrels of emergency stocks can be released by the end of February. Iran's navy said a tanker caught fire after hitting a mine east of Hormuz, which could not be confirmed, and the White House extended a shipping-rule waiver that eases US fuel deliveries.
beats.means: Traders are giving more weight to the expected surplus and emergency stocks than to new war claims. High shipping costs still keep a floor under prices, so oil is drifting rather than falling hard.
beats.fx: A slightly softer oil price takes a little support from the Canadian dollar and helps oil importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: An expected surplus and emergency stocks outweigh an unconfirmed tanker claim.
Softer prices for Canada's main export.

items.watch: Proof from ship trackers or insurers that the tanker was hit; confirmed damage would bring war risk back into oil.

items.headline: Yen steady against euro and dollar after soft Japanese GDP data
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: The dollar started the week at its highest since April 2025 as another Federal Reserve official said inflation still needs work. The yen held near 160 per dollar despite Japan's economy shrinking slightly.

beats.was: US inflation came in hot for October, and Federal Reserve officials have spent the past week saying interest rates must rise again in December.
beats.happened: In early Monday trade in Asia the dollar index sat near 103.4, its highest since April 2025, and the euro was near $1.10. Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid, who does not vote on rates this year, said on Sunday the Fed still has work to do on inflation. Markets put the chance of a quarter-point rise on December 9 at about 94%, while bets on a bigger half-point move eased.
beats.means: Markets now expect about four Fed rate rises by next September, and higher US rates keep drawing money into the dollar. The yen barely reacted to Japan's weak July–September growth, because traders still expect the Bank of Japan to raise rates in December and Tokyo has warned it may step in near 160.
beats.fx: Steady support for the dollar against the euro and gold. The yen is held weak by the gap in rates but capped by the threat of Japanese intervention; the Australian and New Zealand dollars were flat.

impact.why: Another Fed official backs more rate rises; the dollar is at its highest since April 2025.
The euro sits near $1.10, its lowest since April 2025, as the US rate gap widens.
Weak growth and high US rates weigh, but a likely December Bank of Japan rise and intervention threats limit the fall.
More expected Fed rate rises raise the cost of holding gold, which pays no interest.

items.watch: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's speech on Monday: if he sounds less sure about a December rise, the dollar's run could stall.

items.headline: Euro softens below $1.1050 as traders ramp up Fed rate-hike bets
items.story_title: Will the ECB raise rates one last time in December?
items.summary: Most economists in a Reuters survey expect the European Central Bank to raise rates one final time in December. More than a third see another rise early next year, but the euro still slipped toward $1.10.

beats.was: Euro-area inflation is running at about double the European Central Bank's 2% goal, largely because the Gulf war has pushed up energy prices. The bank raised its deposit rate in September and decides again in December.
beats.happened: A Reuters survey of economists, published over the weekend, found most expect a December rise and see it as the last one. Over a third expect a further step in early 2027. Markets already put the odds of a December move at roughly 90%.
beats.means: A December rise is close to a done deal, so it adds little new support. The open question is whether the ECB keeps going in 2027, and most economists think it stops.
beats.fx: The euro gets little lift from news that is already priced, while the Federal Reserve is expected to raise rates in both December and January. The euro sat near $1.10, its lowest since April 2025.

impact.why: A December rise is expected and priced; most see it as the last, so it offers little new support.
The Fed is expected to keep raising rates after the ECB stops.

items.watch: Euro-area inflation for November, due in early December: a sharp drop would weaken the case for any ECB move after December.

items.headline: Iran says it will not wait for the US to attack first
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Iran will not wait to be attacked and suggested US diplomacy is cover to prepare new strikes. He also said UN nuclear inspectors stay locked out for now.

beats.was: Iran and the US have been at war since February, with Iran mining the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil. A June deal opened a 60-day window for talks that has now run out.
beats.happened: Gharibabadi said the Revolutionary Guards are building missiles with longer ranges and will not let the International Atomic Energy Agency, the UN nuclear watchdog, into nuclear sites until Iran's conditions are met. The same day Yemen's Houthis claimed drone hits on pumping stations of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, which Saudi Arabia did not confirm.
beats.means: Tehran is talking tougher just as Trump weighs pausing strikes, so the risk of a fresh round of fighting has not gone away. The East-West pipeline matters because it lets Saudi oil skip Hormuz.
beats.fx: Keeps a war premium in oil, mildly helping the Canadian dollar and hurting oil importers like Japan; adds a little safe-place demand for the Swiss franc.

impact.why: Harder Iranian line and unconfirmed pipeline claims keep supply worries alive.
Threat of new fighting adds some safe-place demand.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so higher prices hurt.

items.watch: Whether Saudi Arabia confirms any damage to the East-West pipeline, and what comes out of Iran's foreign minister's Oman visit on Tuesday.

items.headline: Saudi Arabia intercepts Houthi missiles targeting Riyadh as Iran claims Bahrain drone attack
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Saudi air defences shot down two ballistic missiles that Yemen's Houthis fired at Riyadh on Sunday, plus drones over the oil-rich Eastern Province. Nothing was reported hit.

beats.was: Iran and the US have been at war since February, and Yemen's Houthis, who are backed by Iran, have been firing at Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest oil exporter. Last week Houthi strikes on Saudi energy sites added about $3 to the oil price in a day.
beats.happened: The spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said two Houthi ballistic missiles aimed at the Saudi capital were destroyed, along with drones over the Eastern Province, where most Saudi oil is pumped. It came the same morning Bahrain said it stopped Iranian drones aimed at a US radar site.
beats.means: No damage this time, but the Houthis are now aiming at the capital and the oil region on the same day, and the Group of Seven rich nations condemned the attacks. A hit on Saudi oil sites would matter far more than another failed attack.
beats.fx: Keeps a small war premium in oil, which supports the Canadian dollar and weighs on big oil importers like Japan and the euro area; the Swiss franc gets a little safe-place demand.

impact.why: Attacks on Saudi Arabia keep supply risk alive, though nothing was hit.
More Gulf attacks add some demand for a safe place to hold money.
Firmer oil helps Canada's main export.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so higher prices hurt.

items.watch: Whether any Houthi missile or drone gets through to a Saudi oil site, and whether the Gulf calms around Iran's foreign minister's trip to Oman on Tuesday.

items.headline: Yemen government forces withdraw from area near Bab el-Mandeb Strait, Houthis in control
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces pulled back on Sunday from the area overlooking Bab el-Mandeb, the narrow southern entrance to the Red Sea, leaving Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in control of its shore.

beats.was: Bab el-Mandeb links the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean and carries Gulf oil shipped from Saudi Arabia's Red Sea port of Yanbu, the main way around a mostly shut Hormuz. The Houthis, allied with Iran, have already struck Yanbu and other Saudi oil sites, and the government began an offensive in October to retake the coast.
beats.happened: Southern forces fighting for Yemen's recognised government said they were leaving the Dhubab airport and Bab el-Mandeb area west of Taiz to move toward Aden and defend it, as the Houthis press into the south. Reuters calls it a major setback for the government side.
beats.means: The Houthis now overlook both sides of the Gulf's escape routes problem: with Hormuz mostly shut, the Red Sea is the main bypass, and the group gains more power to threaten it. They have not announced new attacks on ships, so this raises risk rather than cutting supply today.
beats.fx: Adds to oil's war premium and to demand for safe places to hold money such as the Swiss franc.

impact.why: Iran-aligned rebels gain control over the Red Sea route that carries oil around a mostly shut Hormuz.
A wider Gulf war adds demand for a safe place to hold money.
Higher oil prices help Canada's main export.

items.watch: Whether the Houthis warn or attack ships in the Red Sea, and whether shipping firms reroute away from it.

items.headline: Japan Q3 GDP shrinks 0.1% annualised vs +0.3% expected as exports and consumers weigh
items.story_title: Will the Bank of Japan raise rates in December?
items.summary: Japan's economy shrank slightly in July to September, the first fall in a year, as households spent less and exports slipped.

beats.was: The Bank of Japan holds its key rate at 1.25% and markets expect a rise to 1.5% at its December meeting. The dollar has been trading just under 160 yen, a level where Tokyo has stepped in before.
beats.happened: The government's first estimate shows the economy shrank at a 0.1% yearly pace in the third quarter, against forecasts of a small rise. Household spending fell for the quarter and trade subtracted from growth, while business investment rose more than expected. A broad measure of price pressure also came in softer than forecast.
beats.means: A shrinking economy and softer prices give the more cautious Bank of Japan members a reason to wait. Strong business investment keeps the case for a December rise alive, so the figures blur the picture rather than settle it.
beats.fx: Mildly negative for the yen, since anything that delays a Japanese rate rise keeps the gap with US rates wide. The yen barely moved at first.

impact.why: A weak quarter gives the Bank of Japan a reason to delay its December rise.
Keeps the wide gap between US and Japanese rates in place against the yen.

items.watch: Bank of Japan board member Hajime Takata speaks Monday; if he still backs a December rise, the weak quarter matters less.

items.headline: US futures open firmer as Nasdaq leads, oil slips despite Iran tanker claims: 5 things
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Oil opened the week slightly lower and US stock futures rose, even after Iran said a supertanker sank near the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since February, and Iran has claimed several tankers hit mines near Hormuz, the narrow route for much of the Gulf's oil. Brent crude, the world benchmark, ended last week near $96 after two weekly falls.
beats.happened: When trading reopened Sunday evening US time, Brent slipped below $96 and US crude was flat near $87. Iran's claim that a supertanker sank has not been confirmed, and a third US aircraft carrier group is reported to have joined the two already in the region. Gold was steady near $3,890.
beats.means: Traders are not adding much to oil on Iran's claims alone; they want proof of lost supply. A calm open suggests the weekend's attacks did not change the view that supply is running ahead of demand.
beats.fx: A soft oil price takes a little support from the Canadian dollar and eases pressure on oil importers like Japan. Firmer stocks point to a steady mood, which does little for safe places like the franc.

impact.why: Unconfirmed tanker claims did not lift prices at the open.
Slightly softer oil, Canada's main export.
Rising stock futures point to less demand for safe places.

items.watch: Confirmation, from ship trackers or insurers, that a tanker actually sank would bring war risk back into oil.

items.headline: Iran targets Bahrain again as Trump weighs a pause in strikes
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: President Trump has signalled he may hold off on new US strikes on Iran if Tehran and Yemen's Houthis stop provoking, though the US naval blockade of Iran stays in place.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since February, and the US Navy blocks Iran's oil exports. On Thursday Trump said the US no longer needs a deal with Iran and took Vice President JD Vance off the talks.
beats.happened: Reuters reports Trump may pause strikes as long as Iran and the Houthis hold back, while Israeli officials keep pressing Washington to hit Iran again. Over the weekend Iran still claimed drone attacks on a US radar in Bahrain and said more tankers hit mines near Hormuz.
beats.means: It is a conditional pause, not a ceasefire, and the weekend attacks already test the condition. The blockade staying means Iranian oil stays off the market either way.
beats.fx: A pause would take a little war risk out of oil, which mildly weighs on the Canadian dollar and helps oil importers like Japan; a breakdown would do the opposite.

impact.why: Fewer US strikes would ease supply fears, but the blockade and Gulf attacks continue.
Safe-place demand eases only if both sides actually hold back.

items.watch: Whether Iran or the Houthis launch new attacks before Iran's foreign minister visits Oman on Tuesday, which would likely end the pause.

items.headline: Mossad chief returns from US Iran talks as Israeli security cabinet convenes
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Israel's top security ministers met Sunday evening for the first time since the election, after the head of its spy agency briefed Washington on Iran.

beats.was: Israel's caretaker government under Benjamin Netanyahu wants the US to resume strikes on Iran, while President Trump has signalled he may hold off. Gadi Eisenkot, who is forming Israel's next government, has urged restraint.
beats.happened: Mossad head Roman Gofman returned from Washington after briefing senior US officials, including CIA Director John Ratcliffe, on Israel's latest intelligence about Iran. The security cabinet, the group of ministers that can approve military action, then met for the first time since early October. No decision to attack has been announced.
beats.means: Israel is pushing for more military action at the same time Washington talks of a pause, so the two allies are not fully in step. A meeting that could approve strikes keeps the risk of a wider war on the table.
beats.fx: Any sign of new Israeli strikes would lift oil and safe places like the Swiss franc and gold. Silence from the meeting would let that risk fade.

impact.why: A possible new strike on Iran keeps supply risk alive.
War risk adds a little demand for the franc as a safe place.

items.watch: Any statement after the meeting approving action, or US pushback; Iran's foreign minister visits Oman on Tuesday.

items.headline: Fed official supports gradual rate hikes
items.story_title: The Fed's rate rises and the strong dollar
items.summary: Boston Fed President Susan Collins backed steady, modest US rate rises over the weekend and said rates next year may end up a bit higher than she had expected.

beats.was: US inflation has been above the Federal Reserve's 2% goal for more than five years. The Fed's target range is 3.75%-4%, and a quarter-point rise is widely expected on December 9, with another in January.
beats.happened: Collins said a steady, gradual path of rate rises is right for now. She warned that higher long-term borrowing costs could cool demand more than she expects, but said the path of rates next year might be a bit higher than she had thought.
beats.means: Collins is usually one of the more cautious officials, so her nod to a higher path next year adds weight to bets on several more rises.
beats.fx: Supports the US dollar against currencies whose central banks are near the end of their rises, such as the euro and the Australian dollar.

impact.why: A usually cautious Fed official sees rates possibly higher next year than she thought.

items.watch: The Fed's October meeting minutes on Wednesday, and whether other officials echo a higher path for 2027.

items.headline: Iran says supertanker carrying oil sinks in Hormuz Strait
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude sank on Sunday after hitting a mine near the Strait of Hormuz, one of two tankers they say were hit. No one outside Iran has confirmed the sinking.

beats.was: Since the war with the US began in February, Iran has let ships through Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, only with its permission, while the US blockades Iran's ports and escorts tankers. Iran said three tankers hit mines on Saturday.
beats.happened: In a statement on state TV, the Guards said two tankers on an unapproved route hit mines in the south of the strait and one, a supertanker, went down; they gave no names. Separately, the UK Navy's shipping-warning office, relaying Indian authorities, reported a tanker attacked in the Gulf just before the strait, with the crew safe and damage unknown.
beats.means: A sunk supertanker would be the worst ship loss of the recent attacks and a sign that US mine clearing has not made the route safe. Because the claim is unconfirmed and Iran has made similar claims before, markets may wait for ship owners or trackers before reacting fully.
beats.fx: Adds to the war premium in oil when trading resumes Sunday evening US time, which helps the Canadian dollar and costs big energy importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: A claimed sinking and a confirmed tanker attack show the main Gulf oil route is still unsafe.
Dearer oil helps Canada's main export.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so a higher bill hurts.
Gulf escalation adds demand for a safe place to hold money.

items.watch: Whether ship owners or tracking firms name the ship and confirm it sank, and how Brent opens Sunday evening US time.

items.headline: Iranian foreign minister to visit Oman on Tuesday for talks with counterpart
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi will fly to Oman on Tuesday for talks with Oman's foreign minister. It is the first planned diplomatic step after a weekend of mine and drone attacks around the Gulf.

beats.was: Iran and the US have been at war since February. Oman, which sits on the south side of the Strait of Hormuz, has long carried messages between Tehran and Washington, but President Trump said last week the US does not need a deal with Iran.
beats.happened: Iran's state news agency, quoting Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, said Araghchi will hold talks in Muscat on Tuesday. No agenda was given; US coverage links the trip to Oman's role in talks on who oversees Hormuz shipping.
beats.means: A visit is not a negotiation, but it shows a channel for talks is still open even as Iran claims new tanker hits and strikes on Bahrain. Any sign of US involvement would be the first easing since the talks stalled.
beats.fx: A small offset to the weekend's war premium: if the trip produces talk of safer shipping, oil could ease, which would help Japan and the euro area and take a little support from the Canadian dollar.

impact.why: An open diplomatic channel slightly lowers the odds of a long shipping shutdown.
Japan gains if oil import costs ease.
Less war premium in oil means less help for Canada's main export.

items.watch: Whether Oman or Iran says US officials are part of Tuesday's talks, and whether attacks on shipping pause around the visit.

items.headline: Bahrain warns Iran against turning kingdom into 'arena for scores'
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Bahrain blamed Iran for Sunday's drone attacks and said it keeps the right to respond, while Saudi Arabia and the head of the Gulf Cooperation Council, the six-nation Gulf alliance, said an attack on one member is an attack on all.

beats.was: Bahrain, a small Gulf kingdom that hosts the US Navy's regional headquarters, has stayed mostly out of the fighting since the US–Iran war began in February. Late Saturday Iran's Revolutionary Guards said their drones hit a US radar at a Bahraini base.
beats.happened: On Sunday Bahrain's Foreign Ministry rejected Iran's reasons for the attack, said the country will not become a battleground for other people's quarrels, held Tehran responsible and said it would coordinate its defence with fellow Gulf states under their joint defence pact. Saudi Arabia backed Bahrain, and Gulf Cooperation Council chief Jasem Albudaiwi called the drones a direct threat to the whole region. Neither the US nor Bahrain has confirmed that the radar was hit.
beats.means: Words of solidarity are expected, but the talk of joint defence raises the chance that more Gulf states are drawn in if Iran keeps striking. That widens the risk to the region's oil output, not just to ships in Hormuz.
beats.fx: A small extra push for oil and for safe places to hold money such as the Swiss franc; on its own it changes little, since markets already know of the attacks.

impact.why: A wider Gulf front puts more oil output at risk.
Rising regional tension adds some demand for a safe currency.
Any oil premium helps Canada's main export.

items.watch: Whether Gulf states act together against Iran beyond statements, or Iran stops its strikes on Bahrain.

items.headline: Bahrain issues first nationwide alert in months as Iran claims attack on base hosting US helicopters
items.story_title: The Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Bahrain told everyone in the country to take shelter on Sunday after Iran's Revolutionary Guards said their drones hit a US radar at a Bahraini base; Bahrain's military says its air defences stopped the attacks. Saudi Arabia also shot down missiles fired at Riyadh by Yemen's Houthi rebels.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since February, with the US blockading Iranian ports and Iran keeping the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, mostly shut. Bahrain hosts the US Navy's main Gulf base, and Iran claimed a strike on a US radar there on Friday.
beats.happened: Late Saturday the Guards said six drones hit a US air-defence radar at the Riffa helicopter base. Early Sunday Bahrain's Interior Ministry issued its first country-wide alerts in months and explosions were heard, and Bahrain's Defence Force later said it had shot down several Iranian attacks before they reached their targets, its first such interceptions since September. Washington has not commented on Sunday's claim. Saudi Arabia said it destroyed two ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh and drones over its oil-rich Eastern Region.
beats.means: Attacks on a US base and on Saudi Arabia over two days point to the war widening beyond shipping, which makes an early reopening of Hormuz less likely. Bahrain's account suggests little damage, and oil fell last week despite similar news.
beats.fx: Adds to the war premium in oil when markets reopen Sunday evening US time, and to demand for safe places to hold money such as the Swiss franc.

impact.why: Strikes reaching a US base and Saudi Arabia over a weekend raise the risk to Gulf supply.
War news adds to demand for the franc as a safe place to hold money.
Higher oil helps Canada, a big oil exporter.

items.watch: Whether the US confirms damage or answers, and how oil opens on Sunday evening US time.

items.headline: Further interest rate rises needed to tackle inflation, Bank of England's chief economist says
items.story_title: Bank of England: how far do rates rise?
items.summary: Huw Pill, the Bank of England's chief economist, said the bank has further to go after this month's rise to 4% and signalled he would back another quarter-point rise in December. He called market bets on rates near 5% next year not unreasonable.

beats.was: Earlier this month the Bank of England raised its rate to 4%, its first rise in nearly three years, because UK inflation is 3.5% and rising on oil costs from the Iran war. It expects inflation to reach about 5% next spring.
beats.happened: In a Financial Times interview, Pill said the rise was a big step but not the last, that the bank had waited too long to start, and that he expects evidence to justify more rises into 2027. He would not say whether everything markets have priced is justified.
beats.means: A senior official is openly backing more rises, which supports the market view of a December move and rates heading towards 5%. He also said he has not yet seen clear signs of energy costs feeding into wider prices, which is what would force faster action.
beats.fx: Gives the pound some support on rate differences, but it has not stopped a six-day slide against a dollar lifted by expected US rate rises.

impact.why: The Bank of England's chief economist backs more rate rises, in line with what markets already expect.

items.watch: UK October inflation figures, and the Bank of England's December decision.
